idiom_name: flat struct arrays indexed by handles, struct-of-arrays via parallel arrays
implementation_notes: C has no object heap to fight: a struct's members are laid out in declaration order and an array of structs is one allocation, so the classic structure is written directly - one array per record type, plus parallel arrays when only some fields are hot. Records are referenced by index; pointers into the array are the thing to avoid, because reallocation or a swap-based deactivate invalidates them. Padding between members and after the last member is permitted, so use offsetof/sizeof (and _Alignas if a specific alignment matters) to verify the layout you intend; a flexible array member (struct { size_t n; float xs[]; }) keeps a variable-length tail in the same allocation. The practical defaults are calloc for a zeroed pool, a separate active count, and a swap-with-last deactivate to keep the hot prefix packed.
pitfalls: The compiler may insert unnamed padding between members and trailing padding after the last one; check offsets with offsetof before assuming a record size, and reorder or _Alignas fields when the layout is the point.

Any malloc/realloc or growth invalidates stored pointers and even the array base, which is why records must be addressed by index - a cached Particle* is a dangling pointer after the next structural change.
Only some fields belong in the hot struct: putting rarely used data (names, loot tables, dialogue) in the same record bloats every cache line the loop touches.
_Alignas and _Alignof are C11 (attr-spec-seq is C23); on older toolchains alignment has to be arranged by hand, so verify what the build actually guarantees.
